extracted.intended_audience: students, statesmen, constitutional designers, and readers of political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and normative criteria for when to form federations or unions, how to structure their institutions (legislature, courts, distribution of powers), and how a free state ought to govern dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for beneficial admixture of nationalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever really tends to the admixture of nationalities, and the blending of their attributes and peculiarities in a common union, is a benefit to the human race. But, to render this admixture possible, there must be peculiar conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admixture should soften extreme forms and fill intervals without extinguishing types; it requires favorable combinations of circumstances (e.g., relative numbers, civilizational levels, fair governance). Examples: peaceful amalgamation where the powerful govern with tolerable justice (Bas-Breton/France), and mischief where conquest reduces a people to subjection (Greece by Macedonia). Warnings: conquest that reduces people to subjects is a 'sheer mischief' and civilized humanity should prevent it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcomes when a numerically smaller nationality is more advanced
rubrics_metrics.description: If the smaller nationality, supposed to be the more advanced in improvement, is able to overcome the greater ... there is often a gain to civilization, but the conquerors and the conquered cannot in this case live together under the same free institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advanced conquerors subdue a larger, less advanced people, the relationship is likely to be that of rulers and subjects; the success of such absorption depends on whether the conquerors use their superiority to fit the conquered for higher improvement. This topic requires careful governance and may be a benefit or misfortune depending on the use of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions under which a smaller nationality will be reconciled and amalgamate
rubrics_metrics.description: When the nationality which succeeds in overpowering the other is both the most numerous and the most improved, and ... if it is governed with any tolerable justice, and if the members of the more powerful nationality are not made odious by being invested with exclusive privileges, the smaller nationality is gradually reconciled to its position, and becomes amalgamated with the larger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful amalgamation requires just governance and avoidance of exclusive privileges for the dominant group; historical examples include Bas-Breton and Alsatians with France; contrast with Ireland where atrocious governance prolonged separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstacles to blending when nationalities are nearly equal
rubrics_metrics.description: The cases in which the greatest practical obstacles exist to the blending of nationalities are when the nationalities which have been bound together are nearly equal in numbers and in the other elements of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equal-strength nationalities cultivate distinctive peculiarities, revive obsolete customs, regard rival functionaries as tyrants, and view concessions to one as taken from all. Under a despotic external government identity of situation may eventually produce harmony, but if aspiration to free government arrives before fusion, separation is often necessary. Where local position makes joint government inconvenient (e.g., Italian province under foreign rule), breaking the connection is often proper; a federal tie may sometimes be useful but often provinces prefer other alignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: First condition for advising a federation: mutual sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: The first is that there should be a sufficient amount of mutual sympathy among the populations. The federation binds them always to fight on the same side; and if they ... would generally prefer to fight on opposite sides, the federal tie is neither likely to be of long duration, nor to be well observed while it subsists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sympathies useful for federation arise from race, language, religion, and especially political institutions. Example: Swiss union maintained despite religious differences because of common interest; American union damaged by slavery differences that alienated parts of the country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second condition for advising a federation: insufficient individual strength
rubrics_metrics.description: A second condition of the stability of a federal government is that the separate states be not so powerful as to be able to rely for protection against foreign encroachment on their individual strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If member states can defend themselves, they may see union as sacrificing liberty without adequate benefit; lack of sufficient external threat undermines the anxiety needed to preserve the Union and makes dissolution more likely when policy differences arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third condition for advising a federation: absence of marked inequality among members
rubrics_metrics.description: A third condition ... is that there be not a very marked inequality of strength among the several contracting states. The essential is, that there should not be any one state so much more powerful than the rest as to be capable of vying in strength with many of them combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one state is overwhelmingly powerful it will dominate deliberations; if two powerful states exist they will be irresistible when they agree or provoke struggle when they differ. This explains the weakness of configurations like the German Bund where Austria and Prussia skewed outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational modes of a federal union: governments-only vs direct authority
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two different modes of organizing a federal union. The federal authorities may represent the governments solely ... or they may have the power of enacting laws and issuing orders which are binding directly on individual citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The governments-only plan (e.g., German Confederation, Swiss pre-1847, Articles of Confederation experiment) is a mere alliance and precarious; the direct-authority model (U.S. Constitution, modern Swiss Confederacy) where federal acts bind citizens and are executed by federal officers is the only principle likely to produce an effective federation. Warnings: a governments-only federation requires constant readiness to enforce mandates by force and is likely to cause internal wars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for an independent judicial umpire and clear constitutional limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the more perfect mode of federation ... it is evidently necessary not only that the constitutional limits of the authority of each should be precisely and clearly defined, but that the power to decide between them in any case of dispute should not reside in either of the governments ... but in an umpire independent of both. There must be a Supreme Court of Justice ... before whom such questions shall be carried, and whose judgment ... shall be final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every state and the federal government must be suable in these courts for exceeding powers; a supreme federal tribunal must be able to declare laws void that exceed constitutional powers. The practice of waiting for actual cases, hearing full argument, and deciding only what the case requires fosters respectful submission. Safeguard: vigilance is required to guard against deterioration in the quality and impartiality of such courts (example: reference to a judgment impairing confidence—declaring slavery lawful in territories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal powers should include commerce, coinage, weights/measures, and postal system
rubrics_metrics.description: The powers of a federal government naturally extend not only to peace and war, and all questions which arise between the country and foreign governments, but to making any other arrangements which are ... necessary to their enjoyment of the full benefits of union. For example ... mutual commerce should be free ... all custom duties and trade regulations in the United States are made or repealed by the federal government exclusively. ... it is a great convenience to the states to have but one coinage, and but one system of weights and measures ... all post-offices should be under the federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment of these powers to the federal government ensures internal freedom of commerce, uniform currency and measures, and efficient communications. The exact distribution of other powers (e.g., roads and canals) depends on how closely the people wish to draw the federal tie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative structure: bicameralism with population and state representation
rubrics_metrics.description: As regards the mode of adapting these general principles to a federal government, the provision of the American Constitution seems exceedingly judicious, that Congress should consist of two houses, and that while one of them is constituted according to population ... the other should represent not the citizens, but the state governments, and every state ... by the same number of members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents undue power by more populous states and guarantees reserved rights of state governments by making it difficult for measures to pass without approval by both a majority of citizens and a majority of states. Incidental advantage: the mode of election (e.g., nomination by state legislatures for the upper house) tends to raise qualification standards in that house (illustrated by the U.S. Senate).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to choose complete union vs federal union
rubrics_metrics.description: The question may present itself ... whether a country which is determined to be united should form a complete or a merely federal union. The point is sometimes necessarily decided by the mere territorial magnitude of the united whole. There is a limit to the extent of country which can advantageously be governed ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If different parts require essentially different governance so that one legislature and administrative body cannot satisfy them, a federal arrangement or separate legislatures may be necessary. If not, complete union is preferable. Example: England and Scotland retain different legal systems under one Legislature; retention of local institutions can often be constitutionally guaranteed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle for governing dependencies: classification and self-government for European-type colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlying territories ... may be divided into two classes. Some are composed of people of similar civilization to the ruling country, capable of, and ripe for, representative government, such as the British possessions in America and Australia. Others, like India, are still at a great distance from that state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For colonies of European race and civilization, the principle (realized by Great Britain) is to grant fullest internal self-government: representative constitutions, local legislatures and executives, wide freedom in internal affairs, and ready control over lands. Imperial veto is to be sparingly used and only on imperial questions. For small military posts, admit municipal self-government and equal rights elsewhere but not full participation in government tied to military objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local autonomy within a unitary or central government
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever it is not deemed necessary to maintain permanently, in the different provinces, different systems of jurisprudence ... it is always practicable to reconcile minor diversities with the maintenance of unity of government. All that is needful is to give a sufficiently large sphere of action to the local authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical devices include provincial assemblies for local purposes, local assessment of local expenses, apportionment of general expenses to provinces with local levy 'en bloc' to the national treasury. Historical example: French 'pays d'etats' kept a degree of local fiscal autonomy that aided provincial prosperity.
